title: Naomi's Return and Ruth's Pledge
summary: Famine drives Elimelech of Bethlehem, his wife Naomi, and their two sons to Moab, where the sons marry Moabite women and all three men die. Naomi decides to go home and urges her daughters-in-law to stay; Orpah returns, but Ruth clings to her and pledges herself to Naomi's people, her God, and her grave. The two women arrive in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest, and Naomi tells the townswomen to call her Mara, bitter.
story: The book opens “In the days when the judges ruled” (1:1), the period of Judges, which ends in civil war and the refrain that everyone did what was right in his own eyes. Ruth moves from that national chaos to one family, and from warriors to widows. Its first chapter strips Naomi of everything: land, husband, sons, and hope of a future. Yet in the midst of loss, a foreign woman chooses loyalty and faith. The chapter sets up every question the rest of the book will answer: whether Naomi will find a home, whether the family line will survive, and whether the LORD, whom Naomi blames, is really against her. The mention of the barley harvest at the end is the first hint that the answer will be hopeful.
historical:
The setting is Bethlehem in Judah, a farming town about six miles south of Jerusalem, during the period of the judges, roughly the twelfth and eleventh centuries BC. Famines were a recurring danger in a land dependent on seasonal rain, and they drove people to seek food elsewhere, as they drove Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob's sons in Genesis. Moab lay east of the Dead Sea on a high plateau that sometimes received rain when Judah did not. The journey from Bethlehem to Moab would have taken several days, going down to the Jordan Valley and up the other side.

Relations between Israel and Moab were strained. Israel's traditions traced the Moabites to Lot's incestuous union with his daughter (Genesis 19:37), remembered Moab's king hiring Balaam to curse Israel (Numbers 22-24), and recalled Moabite women leading Israelites into the worship of Baal of Peor (Numbers 25). In Judges 3, Eglon king of Moab oppressed Israel for eighteen years. Deuteronomy 23:3 excluded Moabites from the assembly of the LORD. An Israelite family settling in Moab, and sons marrying Moabite women, would have raised questions for a first reader.
cultural:
Widows in the ancient world were among the most vulnerable people. Without a husband or sons, a woman usually had no land, income, or legal protector. Naomi's plight is desperate, and her advice to her daughters-in-law is practical: they are young enough to remarry in Moab, where they have families, but a Moabite widow in Judah would have little chance. Her mention of sons in her womb who could become their husbands (1:11-13) refers to the custom later described in Deuteronomy 25:5-10, in which a dead man's brother married his widow to give him an heir. Naomi points out how impossible that is.

Ruth's pledge would have been understood as more than personal devotion. In the ancient world, a people and its god belonged together; to change peoples was to change gods. Ruth's words bind her to Naomi's people and Naomi's God, the LORD, and her oath calling on the LORD to punish her if she breaks her word shows she is making a solemn covenant commitment. Her promise to be buried where Naomi is buried meant leaving her family's burial place forever, a serious matter in a culture that valued being gathered to one's ancestors.
literary: The chapter is built around the Hebrew verb shuv, to return or turn back, which appears twelve times in various forms. Naomi returns to Judah, urges her daughters-in-law to return to their mothers' homes, and Orpah returns to her people and gods, while Ruth refuses to turn back. The word carries both geographic and spiritual meaning, since elsewhere in the Old Testament it describes repentance. The chapter has a clear structure: the loss in Moab (1:1-5), the dialogue on the road (1:6-18), and the arrival in Bethlehem (1:19-22). The heart of the chapter is dialogue, and Ruth's pledge in 1:16-17 is written as poetry with balanced pairs: “wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” Naomi's final speech plays on names: Naomi means pleasant, and Mara means bitter. Her complaint that she went away full but the LORD brought her back empty (1:21) is the book's starting point.

outline.t: Famine, exile in Moab, and three deaths
Naomi turns home and urges her daughters-in-law to go back
Arrival in Bethlehem: call me Mara

doctrines.note: The chapter begins with famine and death, but also notes that the LORD has visited his people by giving them food (1:6) and ends at the beginning of the barley harvest. God's care is present even in the midst of loss, though Naomi cannot yet see it.

Naomi speaks honestly about her grief and blames the Almighty for her bitterness. The text doesn't rebuke her; it lets her lament stand as part of the story. The Bible gives room for honest complaint to God.

Ruth's pledge to Naomi's God is a confession of faith by a foreigner, made at great cost and with no promise of reward. It shows faith as a commitment of one's whole life to the God of Israel and his people.
Naomi prays that the LORD will show hesed, loyal covenant love, to her daughters-in-law as they have shown it to her. The book will show that prayer answered through the hesed of Ruth and Boaz.

words.note: Hesed, loyal love, kindness, or covenant faithfulness. Naomi uses it in 1:8 when she prays that the LORD will show hesed to her daughters-in-law as they have shown it to the dead and to her. The word describes love that keeps faith within a relationship and goes beyond duty. It is one of the key words of the book and of the Old Testament's description of God's character.

Shuv, to return or turn back, the key verb of the chapter. It describes Naomi's return to Judah, the urging of the daughters-in-law to go back, and Orpah's return to her gods. The prophets use the same verb for turning back to God in repentance. Ruth returns to a land she has never lived in, which makes her return a kind of conversion.

Davaq, to cling, cleave, or stick fast. Ruth clung to Naomi (1:14). The same verb is used in Genesis 2:24 of a man holding fast to his wife, and in Deuteronomy of Israel holding fast to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20). Ruth's clinging is a picture of steadfast loyalty.

Shaddai, usually translated the Almighty. The name is associated with God's power in the stories of the patriarchs (Genesis 17:1) and in Job. Naomi uses it twice in 1:20-21 when she says the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her. She believes in God's power, but experiences it as being turned against her.

christ: The chapter's links to Christ come through the book's larger story and the New Testament's use of it. Ruth, a Moabite, is named in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), one of several women in that list whose stories show God drawing outsiders into his purposes. Her pledge to take Naomi's God as her God foreshadows the gospel's gathering of the nations to the God of Israel, which Paul describes as Gentiles being grafted into Israel's olive tree (Romans 11:17). Naomi's cry that the LORD had brought her back empty is echoed in the Bible's many laments, including the Psalm Jesus quoted from the cross (Psalm 22:1; Mark 15:34). The chapter does not predict Christ, but it begins the story of the family from which he came, and it shows the kind of loyal, self-giving love that the gospel reveals fully in him.

hard.q: Was Elimelech wrong to go to Moab, and were the sons wrong to marry Moabite women?
hard.a: The text doesn't say so directly. Some interpreters, especially in Jewish tradition, have seen the deaths of Elimelech and his sons as judgment for leaving the promised land and marrying foreign women, pointing to Deuteronomy 23:3 and 7:3. Others note that the narrator makes no such judgment, that famine was a legitimate reason to seek food elsewhere (as Abraham and Jacob did), and that the prohibition in Deuteronomy 7 names the peoples of Canaan, not Moab. The book itself shows a Moabite woman embraced by Israel's God and people and becoming the great-grandmother of David, which suggests that its concern is not to condemn these choices but to show God's grace working through and beyond them. Readers disagree on how much blame to assign, and the text leaves the question open.

questions: Naomi said she went away full and came back empty. Where have you experienced loss that made you feel God was against you?
Ruth chose Naomi's people and God with no guarantee of reward. What does her choice teach about loyalty and faith?
Orpah went back, and the text does not condemn her. Why do you think the story presents both choices without judging Orpah?
